Keywords:Protection Motivation Theory、deep vein thrombosis、medication adherence、 Reliability、Validity 1 Introduction Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) are among the most serious and potentially fatal complications folloSwing total hip and knee S arthroplasty (THA/TKA)[[1]]. These two conditionsE represent different stages of R venous thromboembolism (VTE)[[2]] and consPtitute a major threat to postoperative N recovery, quality of life, and patient safety[[3]]. Without adequate prophylaxis, fatal I embolic events can occur in upE to 30% of cases, and survivors may experience L C long-term sequelae such as chronic venous insufficiency, limb edema, and functional I T disability [[4]]. The Rgrowing global demand for THA and TKA, driven by population A aging and improved surgical techniques, has made VTE prevention an increasingly important component of perioperative care. Anticoagulant prophylaxis remains the cornerstone of DVT prevention and is a key indicator of postoperative quality and safety. Evidence-based guidelines e.g., American College of Chest Physicians Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines have demonstrated that appropriate pharmacologic prophylaxis significantly reduces the risk of thromboembolic events after joint replacement[[5]][[6]][[7]]. In China, the implementation of standardized thromboprophylaxis guidelines and enhanced clinical protocols has reduced postoperative DVT incidence from 20.6–58.2% to approximately 2.4–6.5%[[8]], highlighting the importance of systematic prevention strategies. However, despite clear clinical evidence supporting the benefits of ACCAERPTTICEDLE M IANN PURSECSRSIPT anticoagulation, maintaining adherence to prescribed prophylactic regimens after discharge remains a substantial challenge. While adherence rates during hospitalization are generally high due to professional supervision, post-discharge adherence often declines dramatically. International studies report adherence rates ranging from 73% to 90%[[9]][[10]][[11]], whereas domestic research in China shows rates below 56%[[12]]. This drop in adherence significantly compromises the preventive effect of anticoagulant therapy and increases the risk of thrombotic recurrence. Factors contributing to poor adherence include limited understanding of the importance of prophylaxis, concerns about bleeding risks and medication costs, inconsistent patient education, and the absence of professional follow-up after discharge. The promotion of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols, which encourage early ambulatSion and shorten hospital S stays to one to three days [[13]], has further shifted tEhe responsibility for medication R management from healthcare professionaPls to patients and their families. N Consequently, patients’ motivation and self-management ability have become critical I determinants of successful DVT prEevention. L C Previous research has primarily focused on optimizing drug types, dosages, and I T treatment durationRs, with less attention given to the cognitive and behavioral factors A that influence adherence to anticoagulant prophylaxis[[14]][[15]][[16]]. Existing adherence interventions often emphasize clinical management but neglect psychological and motivational determinants of health behavior[[17]]. Although patient education programs have been shown to improve awareness, they do not necessarily translate into sustained behavioral adherence[[18]]. Studies have also indicated that patients’ perceptions of disease severity, treatment efficacy, and self-efficacy significantly influence their willingness to continue prophylaxis[[19]][[20]][[21]]. However, these psychological constructs are seldom systematically evaluated in clinical practice, leaving a gap between behavioral theory and thrombosis management. Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) offers a robust theoretical framework for understanding preventive health behaviors by examining how individuals assess and ACCAERPTTICEDLE M IANN PURSECSRSIPT respond to perceived health threats. PMT posits that protective behaviors are driven by two cognitive processes: threat appraisal and coping appraisal. Threat appraisal includes perceived severity and susceptibility, whereas coping appraisal encompasses response efficacy, self-efficacy, and response cost[[22]]. When individuals perceive a high threat and simultaneously believe they can effectively and feasibly respond to it, they are more likely to engage in protective actions. PMT has been successfully applied to a wide range of health-related behaviors, including vaccination uptake, smoking cessation, and chronic disease self-management[[23]]. It therefore provides a strong theoretical basis for investigating motivation toward anticoagulant adherence after joint replacement surgery. Despite the importance of behavioral motivation in postoperative thromboprophylaxis, there is currently no validated instrumSent designed to measure S patients’ motivation for DVT prevention based on PMET, particularly in the context of R post-arthroplasty care. Existing adherence sPcales either focus on chronic disease N medication or lack theoretical grounding. The absence of a reliable and valid I measurement tool hinders the abEility of clinicians and researchers to systematically L C assess cognitive antecedents influencing adherence behavior. Developing a I T psychometrically sRound scale tailored to DVT prophylaxis could help identify patients A at risk of poor adherence, guide individualized education and behavioral interventions, and improve overall anticoagulant management after discharge. Therefore, the present study aimed to develop and validate the Deep Vein Thrombosis Prophylaxis Motivation Scale (DVT-PMS) grounded in Protection Motivation Theory. This scale seeks to quantify patients’ motivational and cognitive factors related to adherence, providing both a theoretical framework and a practical tool for clinical nursing and patient education. The development of the DVT-PMS not only addresses a significant gap in current research but also offers an evidence-based foundation for designing interventions that enhance patient compliance and reduce the incidence of postoperative DVT. JSON: Name: dvt_pms_pmt_validation Title: Sequential mixed-methods development and psychometric validation of a Protection Motivation Theory–based motivation scale for postdischarge deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis in hip and knee arthroplasty patients Short Hypothesis: A Protection Motivation Theory–based DVT Prophylaxis Motivation Scale (DVT-PMS) will exhibit a stable five-factor structure and meet pre-specified psychometric thresholds (Cronbach's alpha ≥ 0.80, AVE ≥ 0.50, RMSEA ≤ 0.08, CFI ≥ 0.90) when administered to postdischarge hip and knee arthroplasty patients. Related Work: Existing measurement work falls into two groups: (1) generic medication adherence instruments and disease-specific adherence questionnaires developed for chronic conditions, and (2) applications of Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) to predict health behaviors. Limitations of prior approaches include absence of instruments tailored to postdischarge DVT prophylaxis, limited theory-driven item coverage (PMT constructs often incompletely operationalized), small or single-center validation samples, incomplete psychometric evaluation (frequent omission of both EFA and CFA, limited reporting of convergent/discriminant validity such as AVE/Fornell–Larcker or HTMT), and lack of concurrent validity against objective adherence measures. Prior PMT-based interventions demonstrate predictive utility but have not produced a validated DVT-specific motivation scale that captures threat appraisal, behavioral incentives, response efficacy, self-efficacy, and response cost together and that has been cross-validated across independent samples. Abstract: Postdischarge nonadherence to anticoagulant prophylaxis after total hip and knee arthroplasty increases thrombotic risk. We propose a sequential mixed-methods pipeline to develop and validate the Deep Vein Thrombosis Prophylaxis Motivation Scale (DVT-PMS) grounded in Protection Motivation Theory. The pipeline includes literature synthesis and semi-structured patient interviews to generate items, two-round expert Delphi for content refinement, and a multi-site psychometric survey with split-sample exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Validation tests comprise item analysis, content validity indices, EFA (principal axis factoring, oblique rotation), CFA (multiple fit indices), convergent/discriminant validity (AVE, Fornell–Larcker, HTMT), internal consistency, split-half and test–retest reliability, and criterion validity against medication adherence at one month. The main contribution is a PMT-based, empirically validated instrument intended to quantify cognitive antecedents of anticoagulant adherence in post-arthroplasty patients. Expected outcomes are a parsimonious factor structure, robust reliability and validity metrics, and a tool suitable for risk stratification and targeted adherence interventions. Experiments: 1) Data collection: recruit N_total = 700 post-first-time total hip or knee arthroplasty patients from at least 4 tertiary hospitals across distinct regions. Inclusion/exclusion criteria mirror the original study (exclude preoperative DVT, malignancy, recent major bleeding, pregnancy, severe organ dysfunction). Obtain baseline demographics, DVT-PMS responses at 1 month postdischarge, and adherence outcomes (primary: objective refill/prescription pickup or injection administration logs; secondary: validated self-report adherence scale). 2) Sample splits: Randomly partition into Development sample (n_dev = 300) for item analysis and EFA, Cross-validation sample (n_cv = 300) for CFA, and External validation sample (n_ext = 100) for criterion validity and test–retest (2-week re-administration). 3) Item generation & content validity: finalize item pool via literature review, n_interviews ≈ 20 semi-structured patient interviews, and two-round Delphi with ≥10 experts; compute I-CVI and S-CVI; remove items with I-CVI < 0.78. 4) Item analysis: compute item-total correlations, CR (upper vs lower 27%) t-tests; remove items with non-significant discrimination or item-total r < 0.30. 5) EFA (development sample): assess KMO and Bartlett; extract factors via Principal Axis Factoring, Promax rotation; retain factors with interpretability, scree inflection and parallel analysis; keep items with loadings ≥0.45 and cross-loading difference ≥0.20. 6) CFA (cross-validation sample): specify competing models (theoretical 7-factor PMT model vs EFA-derived 5-factor model); estimate with maximum likelihood; report CMIN/DF, RMSEA, CFI, TLI, IFI, PNFI, PGFI; acceptable thresholds RMSEA ≤0.08, CFI/TLI ≥0.90. 7) Convergent/discriminant validity: compute AVE (target ≥0.50), composite reliability (CR ≥0.70), Fornell–Larcker matrix, and HTMT (<0.85). 8) Reliability: Cronbach's alpha for total and subscales (target ≥0.80), split-half reliability (≥0.70), test–retest ICC (≥0.70). 9) Criterion validity: correlate DVT-PMS subscale and total scores with objective adherence (Spearman/Pearson r) and compare means between adherent vs non-adherent groups (t-test or Mann–Whitney); compute AUC for predicting nonadherence. 10) Baselines and ablations: baselines: generic medication adherence scale score and a PMT-7-factor confirmatory model. Ablations: (a) compare full-item set vs reduced item sets (drop items with lowest item-total correlations in steps of 10%), (b) compare 7-factor vs 5-factor models, (c) evaluate influence of merging susceptibility and severity or internal/external rewards. 11) Subgroup and invariance testing: perform multi-group CFA for gender and age groups to test measurement invariance (configural, metric, scalar). 12) Software and thresholds: use SPSS/R for EFA/item analyses and lavaan/AMOS for CFA; two-sided tests with α = 0.05; report effect sizes and 95% CIs. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Sampling bias and generalizability: hospital convenience sampling and regional concentration may produce demographic skew (older, female) limiting external validity. 2) Measurement bias: self-report items subject to social desirability and recall bias; objective adherence sources may be incomplete. 3) Construct conflation: high correlations between PMT subconstructs (e.g., susceptibility vs severity; intrinsic vs extrinsic rewards) may force factor mergers and reduce theoretical granularity. 4) Overfitting: EFA-derived structure may fit the development sample but not replicate; inadequate sample sizes for multi-group invariance test reduce power. 5) Model fit constraints: expected CFA indices may fall short of conventional cutoffs, leaving residual model misspecification. 6) Test–retest reliability limitations: attrition between administrations and short re-test intervals may bias ICC estimates. 7) Language and cultural validity: scale developed in Chinese context may not transfer to other languages/cultures without cross-cultural adaptation. 8) Criterion validity ceiling: low event rates for postoperative DVT and high in-hospital adherence may limit ability to demonstrate predictive validity against clinical endpoints. 9) Operational constraints: dependence on follow-up phone interviews and prescription data linkage may be limited by data access and patient availability.
